mcqs.question: Why does `print(value)` print "Object: hello" instead of "String: hello", given value actually holds a String at runtime?
options: Overload resolution happens at compile time based on the declared type of the variable, not what it holds at runtime
Because String doesn't override toString() by default
Because Java always prefers the Object overload when multiple overloads exist
Because print(String) is private and unreachable from this call site
mcqs.explanation: The compiler picks the overload using value's declared type (Object) at the call site, before the program ever runs — it never inspects the actual runtime object. toString() and access level are irrelevant here, and there's no general 'prefer Object' rule.

mcqs.question: Which of these makes a method an overload rather than an override?
options: Declaring it in a subclass with the exact same parameter list
Making the access modifier more restrictive than the parent's
Changing the parameter list while keeping the same method name
Narrowing the return type to a covariant subtype
mcqs.explanation: A different parameter list with the same name, in the same class, is the definition of overloading. Same parameter list in a subclass is overriding territory, restricting access on override is actually disallowed, and covariant return narrowing is an overriding rule, not an overloading one.

mcqs.question: Which of these is a valid override of a parent's `public Shape area()` method?
options: protected Shape area() — narrowing access is allowed as long as the return type matches
public Shape area(int precision) — adding a parameter is fine as long as the name matches
private Shape area() — access level doesn't matter for overriding
public Circle area() — same name and parameters, with a covariant (narrower) return type
mcqs.explanation: Overriding requires an identical signature with only the return type allowed to narrow covariantly; a Circle-returning override of a Shape-returning method is valid. Access can only stay the same or widen (never narrow), and adding a parameter creates an overload, not an override.

mcqs.question: Why can't a subclass override a parent's private method?
options: Because private methods aren't visible to the subclass at all, so a same-named subclass method is just a separate, unrelated method
Because private methods are always implicitly static
Because Java throws a compile error whenever a subclass declares a method with the same name as a private parent method
Because overriding private methods requires the @Override annotation, which is disallowed on private methods
mcqs.explanation: Private methods have no visibility outside their own class, so there's nothing for the subclass to override — any same-named method it declares is independent. Private methods aren't static, and declaring the same name in a subclass is legal, it just isn't an override.
